Edge-weight Case-dropping Stability

Source: R/casedrop_reliability.R
casedrop_reliability.Rd

casedrop_reliability() measures how stable a network's edge weights are when cases are left out. It re-estimates the network on random subsets that drop each proportion in drop_prop of the cases, compares each re-estimated edge vector with the original, and reports a CS-coefficient for the edge weights: the largest proportion of cases that can be dropped while the correlation between the original and the re-estimated edge weights stays at or above threshold in at least certainty of the iterations (the case-dropping CS-coefficient of Epskamp, Borsboom & Fried, 2018, applied to the edge weights). Beside the correlation it records the mean, median and largest absolute change of the edge weights. The cases are the sequences of a transition network and the rows of the data otherwise. It takes a single network, or a netobject_group or an mcml, whose networks are assessed one by one.

It complements centrality_stability(): that asks whether centrality rankings are stable, this asks whether the edge-weight structure itself is. For an mcml built from an edge list, where each row of the data is one transition, this is case-dropping of edges.

The CS-coefficient is the largest proportion in drop_prop that passes, so it can only be one of the values tried. A smaller proportion need not have passed as well, so look at the correlation at every proportion, not only at the CS-coefficient: summary() gives its mean, median and quantiles (q025, q975) per proportion, and plot() draws it. A correlation near 1 can hide a large change in a few edges, which the largest absolute change (max_abs_dev) shows. Stability under case-dropping says the estimate does not rest on a few cases; it gives no interval for a single edge, which bootstrap_network() does.

Usage

casedrop_reliability(
  x,
  iter = 1000L,
  drop_prop = seq(0.1, 0.9, by = 0.1),
  threshold = 0.7,
  certainty = 0.95,
  method = c("spearman", "pearson", "kendall"),
  include_diag = FALSE,
  seed = NULL,
  target = c("auto", "existing", "all")
)

# S3 method for class 'net_casedrop_reliability'
print(x, digits = 3, ...)

# S3 method for class 'net_casedrop_reliability'
summary(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'net_casedrop_reliability_group'
print(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'net_casedrop_reliability_group'
summary(object, drop_prop = NULL, ...)

# S3 method for class 'summary.net_casedrop_reliability_group'
print(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'net_casedrop_reliability'
plot(x, combined = TRUE, ...)

# S3 method for class 'net_casedrop_reliability_group'
plot(
  x,
  metric = c("correlation", "mean_abs_dev", "median_abs_dev", "max_abs_dev"),
  ...
)

Arguments

x

The network: a netobject or cograph_network that carries its data, or a netobject_group or mcml, whose networks (for an mcml, the macro network and each cluster's) are assessed one by one. A network without data raises an error, and one that rests on a single sequence, or one-hot data with no actor or session, has no cases to drop and raises an error of class nestimate_single_sequence. For the print() and plot() methods: the result of casedrop_reliability() (for print(), also the summary() of a group result).

iter

The number of random subsets drawn for each drop proportion, at least 2. Default 1000.

drop_prop

The proportions of cases to drop, each strictly between 0 and 1, in any order. Default seq(0.1, 0.9, by = 0.1). A proportion that drops no case of a small sample (n * p < 1) is not run (its metrics are NA) and counts as not passing, with a warning of class nestimate_drop_prop_skipped. For the summary() method of a group result: the one proportion to report, which must be one of those the result was built with; a value outside them raises an error listing the available ones. Default NULL there, the middle proportion of the grid (the lower of the two middle ones for an even number).

threshold

The lowest correlation between the original and the re-estimated edge weights for an iteration to count as stable, between 0 and 1. Default 0.7.

certainty

The share of iterations that must reach threshold for a drop proportion to pass, between 0 and 1. Default 0.95. It is the share of all iterations: one in which the correlation is undefined (the edge vector is constant in that subset), or in which the network could not be re-estimated, counts as not reaching threshold.

method

The correlation: "spearman" (default) compares ranks, so it is not affected by the scale of the weights, which often span several orders of magnitude; "pearson" compares the weight magnitudes; "kendall" is Kendall's tau.

include_diag

Whether self-loops are part of the edge vector. Default FALSE.

seed

A number that makes the subsets reproducible. The session's own random stream is left as it was. For a netobject_group or mcml, each network is assessed from the same seed. Default NULL.

target

The cells compared. "existing" compares only the cells that are non-zero in the original network; "all" compares every cell, zeros included, so edges that appear once cases are dropped count. "auto" (default) uses "existing" for unscaled and unthresholded transition networks, where an absent transition cannot appear in a subset, and "all" otherwise. include_diag applies to either.

digits

For the print() method of a single result: the decimal places of the metric table. Default 3.

...

For the print(), summary() and plot() methods: ignored.

object

For the summary() methods: the result of casedrop_reliability().

combined

For the plot() method of a single result: TRUE (default) draws the four metrics as panels of one plot; FALSE returns a named list of four single-panel plots, one per metric.

metric

For the plot() method of a group result: the metric drawn, "correlation" (default), "mean_abs_dev", "median_abs_dev" or "max_abs_dev".

Value

A net_casedrop_reliability object. print() shows the CS-coefficient and the mean and standard deviation of each metric at each drop proportion; summary() returns that table in full, one row per metric and drop proportion; plot() draws the metrics across the drop proportions. A netobject_group or mcml gives a net_casedrop_reliability_group, a named list of one result per network: its print() gives each network's number of cases, number of edges and CS-coefficient, its summary() one row per network at one drop proportion, and its plot() one curve per network. The fields of a single result:

cs

The CS-coefficient: the largest drop proportion at which the correlation reaches threshold in at least certainty of the iterations. 0 when no proportion passes; NA when the original edge weights do not vary (constant up to rounding error, relative to their size), so the correlation is undefined.

summary

A data frame with one row per metric and drop proportion: metric ("mean_abs_dev", "median_abs_dev", "correlation", "max_abs_dev"), drop_prop, and the mean, sd, median, mad, q025 and q975 of the metric over the iterations.

metrics

The per-iteration values: a named list of four matrices, one per metric, with one row per iteration and one column per drop proportion.

correlations

The same matrix as the correlation entry of metrics.

drop_prop, threshold, certainty, iter, method, include_diag

The settings used.

n_cases

The number of cases resampled from: sequences for a transition network, rows of the data otherwise.

n_edges

The number of cells compared, set by target and include_diag.

The resolved target is kept as the result's target attribute.

When the original edge weights do not vary, a warning is given and the result has cs = NA, a summary whose statistics are NA, and metric matrices of NA.

The print() methods return their input invisibly. The summary() method of a single result returns its summary field, described above. The summary() method of a group result returns a summary.net_casedrop_reliability_group data frame with one row per network (named in the row names): n_edges and the four metrics (cor, mean_abs_dev, median_abs_dev, max_abs_dev) at the chosen drop proportion, each written as "mean +/- sd"; its print() names that proportion. The plot() methods return a ggplot; with combined = FALSE, the named list of plots is returned invisibly. A single result is drawn as one panel per metric, the mean across iterations as a line with a band of plus and minus one standard deviation; a group result draws the chosen metric with one line and band per network. On the correlation, a dashed line marks threshold. A result whose CS-coefficient is undefined is drawn as a panel that says so, and in a group such networks are left out and named in the caption.

Details

For each drop proportion \(p\) and each iteration, a subset of \(n - \lfloor np \rfloor\) of the \(n\) cases is drawn without replacement, the network is re-estimated with the input's method, scaling and threshold, and the compared cells of the new weight matrix are set against the same cells of the original. For transition networks the per-sequence transition counts are computed once and summed over each subset; other networks are re-estimated from the subset of rows. A re-estimation that fails, or that loses a node (a variable constant in the subset), leaves the iteration without values; such iterations are counted in a warning of class nestimate_resample_failed and count as below threshold.

With target = "auto", unscaled and unthresholded transition networks compare only the existing edges: an absent transition cannot appear in a subset, and the fixed zeros would inflate the correlation. Association networks and scaled or thresholded networks compare all cells, because a zero original weight can become non-zero once cases are dropped; set target = "existing" to compare only the original edges there.

Case-dropping drops cases at random, so it treats them as independent units. When the cases are nested in actors (several sessions per person), the remaining cases of an actor stand in for the dropped ones, and the CS-coefficient overstates the stability; drop whole actors instead (for example with tna::estimate_cs(actor = )).

References

Epskamp, S., Borsboom, D., & Fried, E. I. (2018). Estimating psychological networks and their accuracy: A tutorial paper. Behavior Research Methods 50(1), 195-212. doi:10.3758/s13428-017-0862-1

See also

centrality_stability(), bootstrap_network().

Examples

set.seed(1)
seqs <- data.frame(
  V1 = sample(LETTERS[1:4], 30, TRUE),
  V2 = sample(LETTERS[1:4], 30, TRUE),
  V3 = sample(LETTERS[1:4], 30, TRUE)
)
net <- build_network(seqs, method = "relative")
es  <- casedrop_reliability(net, iter = 50, drop_prop = c(0.1, 0.3, 0.5),
                      seed = 1)
print(es)
#> Edge-weight Case-dropping Stability
#>   Cases (resampled)     : 30
#>   Edges assessed        : 12 (diagonal excluded)
#>   Iterations / prop     : 50
#>   Correlation method    : spearman
#>   CS-coefficient (r)    : 0.10  (threshold=0.70, certainty=0.95)
#> 
#> Model-level reliability across iterations (mean +/- sd per drop):
#>   drop_prop      p=0.1        p=0.3        p=0.5      
#>   mean|diff|      0.028+- 0.007   0.062+- 0.014   0.095+- 0.018
#>   median|diff|    0.021+- 0.008   0.052+- 0.014   0.085+- 0.023
#>   cor             0.927+- 0.045   0.820+- 0.078   0.688+- 0.161
#>   max|diff|       0.081+- 0.023   0.160+- 0.051   0.241+- 0.056
